packets.key_finding: A nudge that shrouded the minimum-payment autopay option cut the fraction of cardholders paying exactly the minimum by 23% after six months, but did not significantly reduce credit card debt.
packets.methodology: Field experiment on live credit card accounts, six-month follow-up, mechanism analysis via liquidity constraints.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly answers the brief's central question — enrolment/behaviour change from a nudge can move the nominal metric (minimum-only payers) without moving the outcome that matters (debt), which is the exact 'vanity enrolment' worry support raised about the round-up feature.
limitations: credit card debt paydown, not a savings product
shrouding is a different mechanism than opt-in/opt-out/active-choice enrolment
packets.relevance_reason: Consumer, self-directed, liquid financial product showing a default-like nudge changes nominal behaviour without changing the underlying amount, which is the trade-off the brief asks about.
packets.title: The Semblance of Success in Nudging Consumers to Pay Down Credit Card Debt
packets.abstract: We test a nudge in a field experiment on credit cards. The nudge shrouds the autopay enrollment option for cardholders to automatically pay exactly the credit card minimum payment each month. After six months, the nudge decreases the fraction of cardholders who only pay exactly the minimum by 23 percent. However, the nudge does not significantly reduce credit card debt. Nudged cardholders often choose autopay amounts that are only slightly higher than the minimum payment. The nudge reduces autopay enrollment, which increases missed payments. The nudge reduces manual payments by autopay enrollees. Cardholders frequently lacking liquid cash best explains our results. (JEL C93, D12, D91, G21, G51)

packets.key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation defaults raised campaign donations by over $43 million but also increased refund requests by nearly $3 million, with the largest impact on small, inexperienced donors who did not compensate by changing donation amounts.
packets.methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design across political campaign websites that added pre-checked recurring-donation boxes at different times.
packets.why_it_matters: The closest real-world analogue to a preset recurring-financial-commitment default: it quantifies both the enrolment lift and the harm (regret/refunds) concentrated on inexperienced users, exactly the distributional trade-off the brief is asking about.
limitations: political donations, not a savings product
no data on outcomes beyond ~months around the election cycle
packets.relevance_reason: Same choice-architecture mechanism (pre-selected recurring financial default) as the round-up entry/level decision, with effect size and heterogeneity by user experience.
packets.title: Dark defaults: How choice architecture steers political campaign donations
packets.abstract: In the months before the 2020 U.S. election, several political campaign websites added prechecked boxes (defaults), automatically making all donations into recurring weekly contributions unless donors unchecked them. Since these changes occurred at different times for different campaigns, we use a staggered difference-in-differences design to measure the causal effects of defaults on donors' behavior. We estimate that defaults increased campaign donations by over $43 million while increasing requested refunds by almost $3 million. The weekly default only impacted weekly recurring donations, and not other donations, suggesting that donors may not have intended to make weekly donations. The longer defaults were displayed, the more money campaigns raised through weekly donations. Donors did not compensate by changing the amount they donated. We found that the default had a larger impact on smaller donors and on donors who had no prior experience with defaults, causing them to start more chains and donate a larger proportion of their money through weekly recurring donations.
packets.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

packets.key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and framework for when default effects persist or decay downstream, driven by time course of choice, antecedent preferences, and salience of trade-offs.
packets.methodology: Conceptual/theoretical synthesis and research agenda across the consumer default-effects literature; abstract-only.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives a framework for predicting exactly the question the brief asks — whether the entry-default effect on the round-up feature will persist at 6–12 months or decay — and what moderators (salience, antecedent preference) to measure.
limitations: theoretical synthesis, not a new empirical estimate
not specific to financial products
packets.relevance_reason: General consumer-behaviour framework for downstream default persistence, directly usable to design what to measure post-launch.
packets.title: How default choice architecture impacts downstream behavior: A taxonomy, theoretical framework, and research agenda
packets.abstract: Much is known about the immediate effects of default choice architecture and their underlying psychological processes. Yet, significant gaps remain in understanding if, when, and how defaults produce downstream effects on consumer behavior. We resolve conceptual ambiguity around downstream default effects by developing a taxonomy to categorize them and proposing a conceptual framework that illuminates the dynamic interplay of consumers' thoughts and actions with choice architecture as they engage in decision making over time. Applying this framework, we synthesize the current state of knowledge about downstream default effects, producing insights into multiple intersecting factors that modulate them. These include the time course of choice and consumption, consumers' antecedent preferences, and the salience of trade‐offs within and across choices. This theorizing guides our compilation of a research agenda for reconciling inconsistent prior findings and advancing understanding of how defaults interact with individual differences and contextual factors to influence later behavior.

packets.key_finding: Medium- and long-run dynamics undermine the measured effect of automatic enrollment and of default contribution auto-escalation; steady-state saving rates rise by only 0.6% of income from auto-enrollment and 0.3% from auto-escalation, and only 40% of employees escalate on the first date.
packets.methodology: Longitudinal analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating job separation, balance withdrawal, and opt-out from auto-escalation.
packets.why_it_matters: The clearest quantified statement of the support team's objection: default-driven enrolment lift shrinks sharply once turnover, withdrawal, and later opt-out are accounted for — directly bears on whether opt-out enrolment for the round-up feature is a real gain or a vanity metric.
limitations: 401(k) retirement plans, not liquid consumer savings
employer-mediated setting differs from a self-directed app
packets.relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the premise that defaults durably raise saving, with real effect sizes, which is exactly the counter-evidence the brief asked the scan to surface.
packets.title: Smaller than We Thought? The Effect of Automatic Savings Policies
packets.abstract: Medium-and long-run dynamics undermine the effect of automatic enrollment and default savingsrate auto-escalation on retirement savings.Our analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporates the facts that employees frequently leave firms (often before matching contributions from their employer have fully vested), a large percentage of 401(k) balances are withdrawn upon employment separation, and many employees opt out of auto-escalation.Steady-state saving rates increase by 0.6% of income due to automatic enrollment and 0.3% of income due to default autoescalation.Only 40% of those with an auto-escalation default escalate on their first escalation date, and more opt out later.

packets.key_finding: Defaults on financial risk-taking have medium-to-large effects, but implementing a default nudge (especially one the client rejects) lowers ratings of the advisor's honesty and advice quality, and framing of the default question shifts outcomes.
packets.methodology: Three experiments including a representative five-country European sample (n=4207) on default and framing effects in financial advice.
packets.why_it_matters: Direct European consumer-financial evidence that a rejected default carries a reputational cost — exactly the dark-pattern risk the brief flags for EU consumer protection — and that how the default is framed changes uptake independent of its level.
limitations: wealth-management advice context rather than a savings-pot feature
risk-taking outcome, not enrolment/contribution amount
packets.relevance_reason: European, consumer-financial, experimental evidence on when a default is perceived as manipulative — precisely the reputational-risk question the brief raises for opt-out design.
packets.title: Framing the Default Option Right
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT Defaults are powerful nudges to shape individuals' behavior: In three experiments, including a large experiment using representative samples from five European countries (n = 4207), we show that they can significantly affect risk‐taking by medium to large effect sizes. We also show that implementing a default nudge leads to a lower rating of the advice delivered by the wealth manager compared to no default, an effect that has a medium to large effect size. In addition, defaults the targeted individuals refuse result in lower advice ratings. These side effects call for caution before applying nudges and individualized defaults rather than a one‐size‐fits‐all approach. Additionally, we find evidence pointing to two small effects of framing in default presentation. First, asking how much individuals want to invest in the risky asset emphasizes risk. It reduces investment in the risky asset compared to asking them how much they want to leave on the safe account, particularly for more risk‐averse individuals. Second, asking individuals if they want to change a default allocation of 100% in the risky asset leads to more investment in the risky asset than asking them whether they accept such an allocation. Perceived wealth manager honesty appears to mediate the relationship between the default nudge and the rating of the advice.

packets.key_finding: EU DMA-mandated browser choice screens raised Firefox usage by 113% on iOS and 12% on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual, with the effect still growing 15 months after rollout.
packets.methodology: Difference-in-differences design exploiting the staggered rollout of mandatory choice screens on iOS and Android under the EU Digital Markets Act.
packets.why_it_matters: The largest-scale, most recent evidence on forced active choice under EU regulation — directly tests whether an active-choice screen produces durable behaviour change, the core question behind the brief's third design option, at persistence horizons (15 months) the brief specifically asks about.
limitations: mobile browser default, not a financial product
measures which browser is used, not amount of a financial commitment
packets.relevance_reason: Same regulatory mechanism (mandatory forced-choice screen) as the active-choice onboarding option, under the same EU regulatory regime the brief operates in, with long-horizon persistence data.
packets.title: The Effect of Choice Screens on Mobile Browser Usage: Evidence from the EU Digital Markets Act
packets.abstract: Can active choice mitigate the effects of preset defaults? We study this question using a difference-in-differences design around the rollout of the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required iOS and Android to display browser choice screens under certain conditions. We find large effects, with notable differences across platforms: from 15 months after the mandate onward, Firefox usage was 113 percent higher on iOS and 12 percent higher on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual. This gap is consistent with rollout differences, as Android showed choice screens primarily on new devices, whereas iOS also showed them on existing devices.Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.
packets.tldr: Large effects are found around the rollout of the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required iOS and Android to display browser choice screens under certain conditions, with notable differences across platforms.

packets.key_finding: Switching university exam sign-up to opt-out increased nominal sign-ups but had no effect on effortful task completion across many exams, and only helped exam passing for students who were already responsive to university communication.
packets.methodology: Two field experiments changing exam sign-up from opt-in to opt-out, comparing sign-up rates against downstream effortful outcomes (participation, passing) and testing heterogeneity by responsiveness.
packets.why_it_matters: The clearest available demonstration that a default can move the enrolment number while leaving actual effortful engagement unchanged for the majority — precisely the support team's disengagement objection, with a heterogeneity finding (works for already-responsive people, not others) that speaks directly to who is helped versus who is not.
limitations: university exam sign-up, not a consumer financial product
no direct financial-amount analogue to 'money saved'
packets.relevance_reason: Directly tests the brief's central worry — nominal enrolment versus effortful downstream behaviour — with a heterogeneity analysis of who benefits, even though the setting is academic rather than financial.
packets.title: Defaults and effortful tasks
packets.abstract: Abstract Nothing is known about the effectiveness of defaults when moving the target outcomes requires substantial effort. We conduct two field experiments to investigate how defaults fare in such situations: we change the university exam sign-up procedure in two study programs to “opt-out” (a) for a single exam, and (b) for many exams. Both interventions increase task uptake (exam sign-up). Concerning the outcomes which require effort, we find no effects for many exams. For a single exam, the opt-out increases task completion (exam participation) in the study program where the default arguably entails stronger endorsement. Within this program, the effects on successful task completion (exam passing) are heterogeneous: treated students who in the past were willing to communicate with the university (responsive individuals) invest more effort into exam preparation and are more likely to pass the exam than their control counterparts.For non-responsive individuals, we find increased sign-ups but no effects on the target outcomes. Defaults can thus be effective and may be an attractive policy option even when the target outcome requires substantial effort provision. It is, however crucial that the interventions target the appropriate individuals.

packets.key_finding: At-scale UK bank field experiments show automatic enrollment into real-time text alerts reduced unarranged overdraft charges by 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges by 4-8%, implying £170-240 million in annual market-wide savings, though consumers still captured less than half of achievable savings.
packets.methodology: Large-scale randomized field experiments at major UK banks measuring the causal effect of automatic (opt-out) enrolment into alerts.
packets.why_it_matters: This is a genuine consumer-banking automatic-enrolment study (not an employer plan), giving a real effect size for opt-out design in exactly the kind of app-based financial product the brief is building, and shows defaults help but leave real value on the table.
limitations: overdraft alerts are an information nudge, not a savings-level decision
no measurement of persistence beyond the experiment window stated in the abstract
packets.relevance_reason: Directly on-domain: bank-app automatic enrolment with quantified effect size, the closest analogue to the round-up entry decision.
packets.title: Sending Out an SMS: Automatic Enrollment Experiments for Overdraft Alerts
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT At‐scale field experiments at major U.K. banks show that automatic enrollment into “just‐in‐time” text alerts reduces unarranged overdraft and unpaid item charges 17% to 19% and arranged overdraft charges 4% to 8%, implying annual market‐wide savings of £170 million to £240 million. Incremental benefits from “early‐warning” alerts are statistically insignificant, although economically significant effects are not ruled out. Prior to the experiments, over half of overdrafts could have been avoided by using lower‐cost liquidity available in savings and credit card accounts. Alerts help consumers achieve less than half of these potential savings.

packets.key_finding: A randomized reminder nudge in a Brazilian financial app cut credit-card late fees by 14% but raised overdraft fees by 9%, with users who had a history of overdraft use seeing a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
packets.methodology: Field RCT with a financial management platform in Brazil; reminders for upcoming credit card payments tracked against downstream checking-account fee outcomes.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly evidences the support team's concern: a behavioural nudge that looks like a clear average win can concentrate harm on the most vulnerable subgroup, which is exactly the distributional risk the enrolment-default decision needs to be checked against before defaulting everyone in.
limitations: studies payment reminders, not enrolment defaults or contribution-level anchoring
Brazilian credit/overdraft context rather than EU round-up savings
no measure of enrolment persistence or withdrawal behaviour
packets.relevance_reason: Strongest available consumer-financial RCT evidence that a well-intentioned nudge can help most users while harming a concentrated subgroup, bearing directly on C5's distributional and manipulation-risk question for the opt-out design choice.
packets.title: Side Effects of Nudging: Evidence from a Randomized Intervention in the Credit Card Market
packets.abstract: Abstract This paper studies the direct and indirect effects of nudging, by means of a field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil. Reminders for upcoming credit card payments reduced credit card late-payment fees by 14%, but increased overdraft fees in checking accounts by 9%. The unintended effect is concentrated in users with a history of overdraft use. These users experienced a net increase of 5% in total fees, while the rest experienced savings of 15%. The results provide clear insights for nudge design: like any policy action, nudges can have side effects, and one size may not fit all.

packets.key_finding: Active choice, and an 'enhanced active choice' variant that highlights the loss from the non-preferred option, motivated behavior change effectively as an alternative to automatic enrollment, tested in field experiments.
packets.methodology: Series of studies including two field experiments testing active choice and enhanced active choice, building on the Carroll, Choi, Laibson, Madrian & Metrick active-choice design.
packets.why_it_matters: The closest prior work on whether active choice captures most of the enrollment benefit of a default without imposing one, and it proposes a specific enhanced-active-choice framing directly transferable to the app's onboarding screen for decision 1.
limitations: Field experiments in medication adherence and general behavior-change contexts, not consumer financial products
No round-up savings, persistence, or withdrawal data
Small-scale field trials
packets.relevance_reason: Explicit method transfer: the active-choice and enhanced-active-choice mechanisms tested here are the exact onboarding designs the brief is deciding between (C6), regardless of the non-financial application domain.
packets.title: Enhanced active choice: A new method to motivate behavior change
packets.abstract: Abstract High rates of medication non‐adherence have significant public health and economic consequences. In other contexts such as savings behavior, opt‐out policies, in which the alternative preferred by the policy maker is made the default, have gotten great traction but may not be feasible in health care settings. After reviewing previous applications, we present a series of studies, including two field experiments, that test the effectiveness of an alternative, ‘active choice’ policy in which there is no default, but decision makers are required to make a choice (Carroll, Choi, Laibson, Madrian, & Metrick, 2009; Spital, 1993, 1995). In addition, we propose and test a modified version of active choice, that we call ‘enhanced active choice’ that favors one alternative by highlighting losses incumbent in the in the non‐preferred alternative. We recommend Enhanced Active Choice as a complement to automatic enrollment or when automatic enrollment is infeasible or unethical.

alternates.key_finding: In an RCT of 220 participants, all tested nudges — including default options — significantly reduced willingness to contribute to voluntary pension savings relative to a control group, contrary to prevailing international evidence, with the strongest backfire from positive-narrative and default-option nudges.
alternates.methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey (n=220) testing social-norm, framing, default-option, and narrative nudges on pension contribution decisions in China.
alternates.why_it_matters: A direct, explicit counter-example to the 'defaults always help' premise the brief asks us to test, showing defaults can backfire and reduce contribution willingness, with heterogeneity by income, education, and gender that bears on who is helped versus hurt.
limitations: small survey-based sample (n=220), hypothetical choices rather than real product behaviour
Chinese voluntary pension context, culturally and institutionally distant from an EU consumer app
venue is a minor conference-proceedings journal, raising quality concerns
alternates.relevance_reason: The one paper in this batch that directly contradicts the default-effect premise the brief asks the scan to test, with distributional heterogeneity data.
alternates.title: When Nudges Backfire: The Effect of Social Norms, Framing Effects, and Default Options on the Pension Saving Decisions in China
alternates.abstract: This study investigates the impact of behavioral nudgessocial norms, loss aversion framing, default options, and positive narrativeon voluntary pension saving decisions in China. Using a randomized controlled trial administered via an online survey with 220 participants, we examine how these interventions influence both the willingness to contribute and the proportion of income allocated to pension savings. Contrary to prevailing international evidence, our results indicate that all nudges significantly reduce willingness to contribute relative to a control group, with the most substantial backfire effects observed for positive narrative and default option nudges. Furthermore, we identify important heterogeneity effects across income groups and emphasize the moderating roles of education, gender, and financial motivation. These findings underscore the critical importance of cultural, institutional, and individual factors in the design and implementation of behavioral interventions. Policy measures tailored to specific demographic segments and focused on financial education and trust-building are recommended.
alternates.venue: Advances in Economics, Management and Political Sciences

alternates.key_finding: Develops a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations that EU law uses to distinguish acceptable choice architecture from regulable dark patterns, including pre-selected defaults.
alternates.methodology: Doctrinal legal analysis mapping EU dark-pattern law onto a normative autonomy framework. Abstract-only.
alternates.why_it_matters: Directly addresses the brief's reputational-risk concern: it gives the specific line EU regulators draw between a helpful default and a manipulative one, which should shape how the pre-selected multiplier and opt-out exit are worded and disclosed.
limitations: legal/normative analysis, not empirical evidence of user behaviour
no data on enrolment or engagement effects
alternates.relevance_reason: Provides the EU regulatory framework for judging whether the opt-out or preset-multiplier design would read as a dark pattern, which the brief flags as a live risk.
alternates.title: Regulating Dark Patterns
alternates.abstract: Dark patterns have become increasingly pervasive in online choice architectures, encompassing practices like subscription traps, hiding information about fees, pre-selecting options by default, nagging, and drip pricing. Regulators around the world have started to express concerns that such practices are causing substantial consumer detriment. This Article focuses on the legal response to dark patterns in the European Union. It provides the first comprehensive mapping of European Union laws expressly addressing dark patterns. The Article argues that these laws protect biased consumers and adopt autonomy as a normative lens to assess dark patterns. Consequently, regulating dark patterns in European Union law means regulating for autonomy. This normative lens is under-researched. This Article addresses this gap in research with two principle contributions. First, it works out a specific conception of autonomous decision-making, rooted in the paradigm that providing consumers with information enables consumers to make an informed decision. Second, the Article offers a novel normative classification for dark patterns in online choice architectures. It develops a taxonomy encompassing six categories of autonomy violations, specifically tailored for the assessment and regulation of dark patterns that exploit consumer behavioral biases. These categories serve multiple purposes. They uncover and make explicit the autonomy violations addressed by existing European Union laws. They delineate the contentious line between acceptable influences on consumer decision-making and autonomy violations that may warrant regulation in online choice architectures. They also provide policymakers in the EU and elsewhere with a framework when deliberating the regulation of other instances of dark patterns.

alternates.key_finding: Default enrollment in Medicare Part D has large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization; beneficiary passivity is remarkably insensitive even to substantial losses from staying in a bad default, and active-choice variation is driven by transitory shocks rather than attentiveness.
alternates.methodology: Three natural experiments with random assignment to default options in a large administrative health-insurance dataset.
alternates.why_it_matters: Strong evidence that default persistence is not conditional on the default being 'good' — relevant caution for whether a pre-set multiplier will simply stick regardless of fit, and that active-choice behaviour may not reflect genuine preference.
limitations: government health-insurance program, not a consumer fintech product
low-income beneficiary population differs from the app's user base
alternates.relevance_reason: Rigorous natural-experiment evidence on default persistence and the (in)sensitivity of passivity, directly bearing on whether the round-up default would similarly entrench regardless of fit.
alternates.title: The Behavioral Foundations of Default Effects: Theory and Evidence from Medicare Part D
alternates.abstract: We show in two natural experiments that default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization of low-income beneficiaries. The implications of this phenomenon for welfare and optimal policy depend on the sensitivity of passivity to the value of the default option. Using random assignment to default options, we show that beneficiary passivity is extremely insensitive, even when enrolling in the default option would result in substantial drug consumption losses. A third natural experiment suggests that variation in active choice is driven by random transitory shocks rather than the inherent attentiveness of some beneficiaries.

alternates.key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment raised participation above 85% at three firms; about 80% of new enrollees initially accepted both the low default contribution rate and default fund, and half still did so after three years.
alternates.methodology: Multi-year administrative panel data from three large U.S. firms comparing automatic vs. opt-in 401(k) enrollment.
alternates.why_it_matters: Gives the clearest quantified persistence-of-anchoring evidence (default settings still holding at three years) directly bearing on both C2 and C3, and a caution that default-driven participation gains can be offset by low default levels — a check against assuming defaults straightforwardly help.
limitations: Employer 401(k) retirement plans, not a liquid consumer savings app
No active-choice comparison arm
Persistence measured over years, not the weeks/months timeframe relevant to round-up disengagement
alternates.relevance_reason: The classic foundational study quantifying both default-driven enrollment (C1) and long-run anchoring on default settings (C2, C3), against which later default-effect claims are measured.
alternates.title: For Better or For Worse: Default Effects and 401(k) Savings Behavior
alternates.abstract: In the last several years, many employers have decided to automatically enroll their new employees in the company 401(k) plan. Using several years of administrative data from three large firms, we analyze the impact of automatic enrollment on 401(k) participation rates, savings behavior, and asset accumulation. We find that although employees can opt out of the 401(k) plan, few choose to do so. As a result, automatic enrollment has a dramatic impact on retirement savings behavior: 401(k) participation rates at all three firms exceed 85%, but participants tend to anchor at a low default savings rate and in a conservative default investment vehicle. We find that initially, about 80% of participants accept both the default savings rate (2% or 3% for our three companies) and the default investment fund (a stable value or money market fund). Even after three years, half of the plan participants subject to automatic enrollment continue to contribute at the default rate and invest their contributions exclusively in the default fund. The effects of automatic enrollment on asset accumulation are not straightforward. While higher participation rates promote wealth accumulation, the low default savings rate and the conservative default investment fund undercut accumulation. In our sample, these two effects are roughly offsetting on average. However, automatic enrollment does increase saving in the lower tail of the savings distribution by dramatically reducing the fraction of employees who do not participate in the 401(k) plan.

alternates.key_finding: At a 12% default contribution rate, 25% of employees had not opted out after 12 months, versus roughly half staying at typical lower defaults, and low-income employees were disproportionately anchored to a suboptimal rate.
alternates.methodology: Administrative data from a single employer's retirement plan with a very high default, compared against a literature review of lower-default plans. Abstract-only for effect sizes.
alternates.why_it_matters: Directly tests whether the level of a preset default anchors people to a possibly-suboptimal contribution level, which bears on whether to pre-select 1x/2x/5x round-up.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a consumer app the employer does not mediate
single-employer natural experiment
alternates.relevance_reason: Closest available quantitative evidence on how the specific level of a default anchors contribution behaviour and who it disadvantages.
alternates.title: Automatic Enrollment with a 12% Default Contribution Rate
alternates.abstract: We study a retirement savings plan with a default contribution rate of 12% of income, which is much higher than previously studied defaults. Twenty-five percent of employees had not opted out of this default 12 months after hire; a literature review finds that the corresponding fraction in plans with lower defaults is approximately one-half. Because only contributions above 12% were matched by the employer, 12% was likely to be a suboptimal contribution rate for employees. Employees who remained at the 12% default contribution rate had average income that was approximately one-third lower than would be predicted from the relationship between salaries and contribution rates among employees who were not at 12%. Defaults may influence low-income employees more strongly in part because these employees face higher psychological barriers to active decision making.
